II. 
Purpose of Testimony and Overview of Filing 
17 
Q. 
What is the purpose of the Panel’s testimony? 
18 
A. 
The purpose of the Panel’s testimony is to support KEDNY’s request to 
19 
increase its gas delivery rates.  In support of this request, the Panel will: 
20 


--- Page 14 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 11 of 132 
(i) 
present KEDNY’s historic and forecast financial data for various 
1 
periods in a manner consistent with the Commission’s regulations and 
2 
policies; 
3 
(ii) 
describe KEDNY’s forecast of operation and maintenance (“O&M”) 
4 
expenses, as well as adjustments to those expenses that were made to 
5 
normalize the historic test year amounts; 
6 
(iii) 
describe KEDNY’s efforts to reduce its cost of service and detail how 
7 
savings related to specific Company productivity initiatives were 
8 
reflected in the filings; 
9 
(iv) 
discuss the development of KEDNY’s gas rate base; 
10 
(v) 
support KEDNY’s forecast of regulatory deferral balances, including 
11 
the proposal to aggregate and net together certain regulatory asset and 
12 
liability accounts and recover the net balance in base rates over a 10-
13 
year amortization period; and  
14 
(vi) 
describe proposed treatment for deferrals that the Commission has 
15 
previously adopted, as well as proposed new deferral mechanisms.  
16 
 
17 
The Panel will also describe the Company’s efforts in connection with the 
18 
preparation of this rate filing to review the accuracy of costs in the historic test 
19 
year and to appropriately normalize these results for known and measurable 
20

Q. 
What is the historic test year in these proceedings?   
20 
A. 
The historic test year in these proceedings is the twelve months ended 
21 
December 31, 2022 (“Historic Test Year”).  The Historic Test Year data 
22 
consists of the costs recorded on the books of KEDNY, including: (i) costs 
23 
incurred directly by the Company; (ii) costs charged to KEDNY from National 
24 
Grid Service Company and National Grid Engineering & Survey, Inc. 
25 
(collectively, the “Service Company”); and (iii) costs charged to KEDNY from 
26 
other affiliated companies.   
27 
 
28 


--- Page 17 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 14 of 132 
Q. 
What Historic Test Year and Rate Year information is the Company 
1 
presenting? 
2 
A. 
The Company is presenting operating results for the Historic Test Year and 
3 
forecast data for the rate year, which is the twelve months ending March 31, 
4 
2025 (“Rate Year”).  In addition, the Company is including forecast data for the 
5 
twelve months ending March 31, 2026 (“Data Year 1”), March 31, 2027 (“Data 
6 
Year 2”), and March 31, 2028 (“Data Year 3”) (collectively, the “Data Years”) 
7 
for informational purposes and to facilitate the possibility of a multi-year rate 
8 
settlement in these proceedings.  The forecast data provides the basis for 
9 
computing the revenue requirement for the Rate Year and Data Years in these 
10 
proceedings.  The information presented in these filings is consistent with that 
11 
required under the Commission’s “Statement of Policy on Test Periods in Major 
12 
Rate Proceedings.” 
13 
 
14 
Q. 
What are KEDNY’s revenue requirements and associated revenue 
15 
deficiencies based on current rates? 
16 
A. 
Based on the cost of services set forth in the Company’s filing, for the Rate 
17 
Year, KEDNY’s revenue deficiency is $414.222 million, based on a 9.8 percent 
18 
return on equity and a 48 percent common equity ratio, as supported by 
19 
Company Witness Joshua Nowak and the Capital Structure Panel.  If a four-
20 
year settlement is reached, the Company proposes that a return on equity of 10.3 
21 


--- Page 18 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 15 of 132 
percent be used to calculate the revenue requirement, as supported by 
1 
Mr. Nowak.  
2 
 
3 
In the absence of the rate relief requested in this filing, KEDNY projects that it 
4 
would earn a rate of return in the Rate Year of 2.96 percent, which equates to a 
5 
return on equity of 1.18 percent – well below KEDNY’s currently authorized 
6 
return of 8.8 percent.   
7 
 
8 
Q. 
How does KEDNY propose to address the current revenue deficiencies? 
9 
A. 
The Company is proposing to increase base delivery rates, which were last set 
10 
in the 2019 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases, to permit the Company to recover 
11 
its costs of providing service and allow the Company an opportunity to earn a 
12 
fair return.  As part of a multi-year settlement, the Company would consider 
13 
levelizing the proposed rate increase to ease the impact on customers.   
14 
 
15

proceedings, comprising:

Trend Analysis 
4 
Q. 
Did the Company compare Historic Test Year operations and maintenance 
5 
(“O&M”) costs with prior period costs? 
6 
A. 
Yes. The Company performed an analysis to look at changes in expenses 
7 
incurred by the Company from calendar year (“CY”) 2018 through the Historic 
8 
Test Year (the 12 months ended December 31, 2022).  The purpose of the 
9 
review was to look at trends in costs by functional area incurred by the 
10 
Company directly, as well as from the Service Company and affiliates that 
11 
charge the Company.  The Company examines its total cost of providing service 
12 
to draw meaningful conclusions regarding year-over-year variations.  The 
13 
Company conducted this examination by combining: (i) costs incurred directly 
14 
by the Company, (ii) costs charged to the Company from the Service Company, 
15 
and (iii) costs charged to the Company from other affiliates.  The analysis of 
16 
costs based on the combination of direct and indirect charges highlights and 
17 
clarifies the factors driving cost increases and decreases by removing the impact 
18 
of organizational changes that merely shift costs rather than actual changes in 
19 
costs from year-to-year.  Exhibit __ (RRP-2), Schedule 4 presents a comparison 
20 
of total O&M costs for the period from CY 2018 through the Historic Test Year. 
21

Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY)

3

4

Q.  
How does the Company determine whether the costs it incurs from the 
1 
Service Company are reasonable? 
2 
A. 
The Company validates the accuracy of allocations, updates the calculations 
3 
that support the allocation methods, and validates that the overall spending 
4 
levels for the departments are reasonable.  The allocations are validated to 
5 
ensure they follow the Company’s Cost Allocation Compliance Program and 
6 
the overall spending levels are set and reviewed during the annual budget 
7 
planning process, which includes financial leadership and jurisdictional 
8 
president reviews.   
9 
 
10 
The Company performs reviews and controls to ensure the allocations are 
11 
accurate and in agreement with the Company’s Cost Allocation Compliance 
12 
Program.  Reviews include vendor payments, employee expenses, and manual 
13 
journal entries that originate from the Service Company.  These reviews 
14 
validate that the costs are allocated to the companies that cause the costs to be 
15 
incurred.  If errors are found, the Company will record correcting entries.   
16 
 
17 
The Company recalculates rates used for the different allocation methods 
18 
annually.  Employee headcounts, customer counts, and financial data are 
19 
gathered and used as support for the different allocation methods.  Director level 
20 
reviews are performed as a final check to ensure the accuracy of the updates. 
21 


--- Page 35 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 32 of 132 
 
1 
To ensure the spending levels for all departments (including those originating 
2 
from the Service Company) are properly funded, the Company performs 
3 
reviews during the budget planning process.  The funding levels are compared 
4 
to prior year results with any significant changes being reviewed and agreed 
5 
upon.  These funding levels are reviewed by the Jurisdictional President and the 
6 
leaders of each function to ensure they reflect the service levels required.  
7 
Throughout the year reports are generated monthly that show functional 
8 
spending for each Company by function.  Monthly performance results are 
9 
reviewed in total with the New York President and leaders of each function to 
10 
ensure performance is aligned with expected levels of funding and deviations 
11 
are discussed.  Reviews can result in corrective action when necessary if a 
12 
department begins to exceed agreed upon funding levels. 
13 
 
14 
The combination of the controls in place that validate allocations align with the 
15 
Company’s Cost Allocation Compliance Program, the annual rate methodology 
16 
updates and the annual budget planning process work together to ensure the 
17 
costs incurred from the Service Company are reasonable.   
18

IV. 
O&M Expenses 
1 
Q. 
Please explain the methodology for developing the forecast of O&M 
2 
expenses in the Rate Year and Data Years. 
3 
A. 
To develop the O&M forecasts, the Company began by determining the costs 
4 
incurred in the Historic Test Year for the various expense types.  Next, the 
5 
Company reviewed Historic Test Year charges to determine whether specific 
6 
costs should be normalized, for example, as out-of-period or one-time charges.  
7 
The inflation factors set forth in Exhibit __ (RRP-8) were then applied to the 
8 
majority of expense types to forecast the Rate Year and Data Years.  Forecasts 
9 
of certain expenses were developed using a more comprehensive methodology 
10 
than adjusting for inflation.  For example, labor expense was developed by 
11 
annualizing the monthly and weekly employees on payroll as of the end of the 
12 
Historic Test Year, adjusting for known changes to the employee headcount, 
13 
and applying contractual and projected wage increases to forecast the Rate Year 
14 
and Data Years.  Additionally, the Company adjusted forecast O&M expenses 
15 
to reflect incremental work projected for the Rate Year or costs associated with 
16 
new initiatives.   
17 
 
18 
Q. 
What assumptions did the Company make regarding non-labor inflation? 
19 
A. 
Except where specifically identified otherwise, the Company applied the non-
20 
labor inflation factor of 6.54 percent to all non-labor expenses in the Historic 
21 


--- Page 37 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 34 of 132 
Test Year to forecast the Rate Year.  This factor is equivalent to a 2.91 percent 
1 
average annual increase between the Historic Test Year and the Rate Year.  The 
2 
Company applied the non-labor inflation factor of 1.93 percent to forecast Data 
3 
Year 1, 1.81 percent to forecast Data Year 2, and 1.77 percent to forecast Data 
4 
Year 3.  These factors represent the forecast change in the Chained Price Index 
5 
GDP Implicit Price Deflator (“GDPIPD”) obtained from Moody’s, as provided 
6 
in Exhibit __ (RRP-8).  The Panel addresses calculation of the non-labor 
7 
inflation factor later in its testimony.   
8 
 
9 
Q. 
What is the basis for the allocations between expense and capital in the 
10 
Rate Year and Data Years?   
11 
A. 
Except as otherwise indicated, costs in the Rate Year and Data Years are 
12 
allocated between expense and capital consistent with their Historic Test Year 
13 
allocation. 
14 
 
15 
Q. 
Please explain Exhibit __ (RRP-3). 
16 
A. 
Exhibit __ (RRP-3) includes 43 schedules and a summary that shows total 
17 
adjusted departmental O&M expense for the Historic Test Year of $608.336 
18

Q. 
Please explain the derivation of the Provider Company O&M expense on 
10 
Pages 1 through 4 of each Schedule of Exhibit __ (RRP-3). 
11 
A. 
There are several National Grid entities that provide services directly and 
12 
indirectly to KEDNY.  The charges associated with those services are either 
13 
directly charged to KEDNY or allocated among the various National Grid 
14 
affiliates (including KEDNY) that receive the services.  For example, when the 
15 
Service Company performs a service for the benefit of a single company, that 
16 
company is directly charged for that service.  If the service is for the benefit of 
17 
multiple companies, however, the charge is allocated to those companies using 
18 
an appropriate allocator.  Pages 1 through 3 detail charges to KEDNY from the 
19 
Provider Companies, including the Service Company.

Q. 
Please describe how the Service Company charged KEDNY for services 
7 
during the Historic Test Year. 
8 
A. 
Service Company charges were either directly charged to KEDNY or, when a 
9 
service was performed for multiple affiliates, charges were aggregated and 
10 
allocated to all affiliates that benefited from the service using approved 
11 
allocation methodologies.  These allocations have been developed to 
12 
accommodate the different types of costs that are charged by the Service 
13 
Company.  
14 
 
15 
 
The allocators are based on cost causation principles and are designed to 
16 
maximize use of direct allocation codes where charges have been incurred for 
17 
the direct benefit of a single company.  When it is not appropriate to use a direct 
18 
allocation code, a cost causative code is assigned based on the appropriate 
19 
causation driver.  Where it is not appropriate to use a direct or cost causative 
20 
code, then a general allocator is used.  The general allocator used by the Service 
21 


--- Page 41 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 38 of 132 
Company is based on a three-point model using Net Margin, Net Plant, and Net 
1 
O&M expense.  These allocation principles are set forth in National Grid’s Cost 
2 
Allocation Manual.

A. 
KEDNY accounts for pension and OPEB costs in accordance with the 
19 
Commission’s “Statement of Policy on Pensions and Other Postretirement 
20 
Benefits Other Than Pensions,” issued September 7, 1993, in Case 91-M-0890 
21 


--- Page 50 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 47 of 132 
(“P&OPEB Policy”). Under the P&OPEB Policy, KEDNY is required to use 
1 
internal reserve accounting to account for any amount of pension and OPEB 
2 
expenses recovered in rates but that are either not deposited in an external trust 
3 
fund or paid out as benefits.  Amounts reflected in KEDNY’s internal reserve 
4 
accrue carrying costs at the Commission-authorized pre-tax cost of capital. 
5 
 
6 
Q.  
How are OPEB and pension expenses currently recovered in KEDNY’s 
7 
rates? 
8 
A.  
KEDNY’s current rate allowances for OPEB and pension expenses are $(3.339) 
9 
million and $(1.044) million, respectively. The Company reconciles the rate 
10 
allowances with the actual OPEB and pension expenses it books for GAAP 
11 
purposes and defers under or over recoveries pursuant to the Commission’s 
12 
P&OPEB Policy. 
13 
 
14 
Q.  
What amount of OPEB and pension expenses is the Company proposing to 
15 
include in the Revenue Requirements in this case for the Rate Year and 
16 
Data Years? 
17 
A.  
As shown in Schedules 11 and 16, KEDNY is proposing to set the rate 
18 
allowance for its pension and OPEB expenses in the Rate Year to $0 for all 
19 
years. The Company is proposing allowances set to $0 for OPEB and pension 
20 
expense because the forecasts of pension and OPEB expenses provided by its 
21 


--- Page 51 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 48 of 132 
actuary, Aon Hewitt (“Aon”), and detailed in Schedules 11 and 16, respectively, 
1

2 
reflects the well-funded nature of the pension and OPEB trusts, which is the 
3 
result of historic contributions, favorable asset returns and National Grid’s 
4 
ongoing efforts to contain pension and OPEB costs.   
5 
 
6 
Q. 
Given that the pension and OPEB expenses as determined by the 
7 
Company’s actuary are negative, why is the Company not proposing to 
8 
reflect negative pension and OPEB expenses in its revenue requirement? 
9 
A. 
The assets in the OPEB and pension trusts cannot be withdrawn without 
10 
significant penalty under the Internal Revenue Code.  Thus, including negative 
11 
pension and OPEB expenses in the Company’s revenue requirement would 
12 
adversely impact the Company’s cash flow because the Company would not 
13 
be able to offset the negative expense with cost-effective withdrawals from the 
14 
pension and OPEB trusts.     
15 
 
16

Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY)

Q. 
Please describe 53rd week labor costs. 
13 
A. 
Every five years there is an additional, or 53rd, pay week.  Therefore, an amount 
14 
equal to one-fifth of the weekly cost (i.e., one day) is added to the labor cost to 
15 
reflect the normalized cost of the 53rd week.  Fifty-third week labor costs are 
16 
associated with any employee who is paid weekly.  Typically, these are 
17 
represented employees.  The 53rd week labor costs are added to the total Rate 
18 
Year represented labor costs found on Pages 10 through 13 of Schedule 23.   
19 
 
20 


--- Page 68 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 65 of 132 
Q. 
How were 53rd week labor costs calculated? 
1 
A. 
Fifty-third week labor costs were calculated by taking the estimated annual Rate 
2 
Year labor costs for weekly paid employees divided by 2,080 hours and 
3 
multiplied by eight hours.  The 2,080 hours represents the total number of hours 
4 
worked in a normal calendar year and the eight hours represents the normal 
5 
work hours in a day (i.e., one-fifth of the week).  The calculation was performed 
6 
by salary band for full time represented employees and part time represented 
7 
employees.

Q.

6 
A. 
Transportation lease expense consists of vehicles on lease in the Historic Test 
7 
Year that will remain on lease through the Rate Year, and vehicles on lease in 
8 
the Historic Test Year that will be replaced before or during the Rate Year.  In 
9

10 
costs of additional vehicle leases needed to achieve the proposed incremental 
11 
work plan presented in this case.  Finally, the Company included two 
12 
adjustments to transportation lease expense related to electrification of a portion 
13 
of the Company’s fleet: an adjustment to reflect the incremental cost associated 
14 
with replacing certain internal combustion engine (“ICE”) vehicles with electric 
15 
vehicles (“EVs”) and an adjustment to add lease expense for twelve mobile 
16 
chargers, which is split between KEDNY and KEDLI.  The Company’s fleet 
17 
electrification program is discussed more fully in the GIOP testimony.

Q. 
How did the Company develop the forecast for transportation lease 
1 
expense? 
2 
A. 
The Company began with the vehicle inventory as of December 31, 2022.  From 
3 
that, the Company first forecast the lease expense for existing leases as of 
4 
December 31, 2022 through the term of the leases.  Second, the Company added 
5

6 
be acquired prior to or in the Rate Year and Data Years.  In general, vehicles 
7

8

9

10 
adjustment to reflect the incremental cost associated with replacing certain ICE 
11 
vehicles with EVs.  Finally, the Company reduced the forecast by estimated 
12 
gains to be received from sales of replaced vehicles at auction.

Q. 
Please explain how transportation lease expense is calculated. 
15 
A. 
Estimated delivery dates are established for the replacement and additional 
16 
vehicles along with projected acquisition costs.  Lease expenses are then 
17 
calculated using the acquisition cost, term of the lease, and projected interest 
18 
rate provided by the leasing company.

--- Page 71 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 68 of 132 
Q. 
Why did the Company not simply adjust the Historic Test Year for 
1 
inflation to forecast the Rate Year and Data Years? 
2 
A. 
The Company does not believe that adjusting for inflation provides an accurate 
3 
projection of activity in the Rate Year and Data Years.  Transportation lease 
4 
expense is affected by changes in the Company’s fleet.  Specifically, increases 
5 
or decreases in lease expense result from vehicles being removed, replaced, or 
6 
added to the Company’s fleet.  In addition, the Company’s fleet is comprised 
7 
of many different types of vehicles and equipment.  These vehicles vary in costs 
8 
and lease terms.  The Company’s forecast takes into account these known and 
9 
measurable changes and, therefore, provides a more accurate and reasonable 
10 
forecast than simply adjusting for inflation.  
11 
 
12 
Transportation Motor Fuel Expense 
13 
Q. 
How did the Company develop the forecast for motor fuel expense? 
14 
A. 
Motor fuel expense was calculated by multiplying the forecast prices from the 
15 
New York Mercantile Exchange by the level of fuel consumption in the Historic 
16 
Test Year.  To determine the forecast of compressed natural gas (“CNG”), the 
17 
Company utilized the 2022 Clean Cities Alternative Fuel Price Report issued 
18 
by the US Department of Energy, which sets forth the average difference 
19 
between retail diesel prices and the CNG price per gallon equivalent by state.  
20 
For New York State, the midpoint of the difference was $1.045.  The Company 
21 


--- Page 72 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 69 of 132 
subtracted this amount from the forecast retail diesel rates to arrive at the CNG 
1 
forecast.  The Company also made a discrete adjustment to Historic Test Year 
2 
gallons of fuel consumption used to forecast Rate Year motor fuel expense by 
3 
removing gallons associated with ICE vehicles operated in the Historic Test 
4 
Year that are forecast to be replaced with EVs in the Rate Year and Data Years.

Q. 
How much SIR cost does KEDNY currently recover annually through base 
1 
rates? 
2 
A. 
KEDNY currently recovers (i) historic, unrecovered SIR expenditures in an 
3 
amount equal to the annual amortization of the SIR deferral balance as of 
4 
December 31, 2016 and (ii) forecast SIR costs of $70.919 million (the “Forecast 
5 
Rate Allowance”).  Each year, KEDNY fully reconciles its actual SIR expense 
6 
to the Forecast Rate Allowance.  Any under or over expenditures are deferred 
7 
for future refund to or recovery from customers (except for expenditures and 
8 
recoveries associated with the Citizens site).   
9 
 
10 
Additionally, if the difference between actual SIR expense and the Forecast 
11 
Rate Allowance exceeds $25 million on a cumulative basis, KEDNY is 
12 
authorized to recover through the SIR Recovery Surcharge (i) the difference 
13 
between actual SIR expense and the Forecast Rate Allowance and (ii) any 
14 
amount that was not recovered in the prior rate year’s SIR Recovery Surcharge 
15 
(if triggered) because the cumulative difference between actual SIR costs and 
16 
the Forecast Rate Allowance did not exceed the $25 million threshold and/or 
17 
the amount would have increased KEDNY’s aggregate revenues by more than 
18 
two percent.

IV. 
Efficiency and Productivity Cost Reductions 
1 
Q. 
Please describe National Grid’s efforts to reduce costs. 
2 
A. 
National Grid is committed to continuously identifying opportunities to be more 
3 
efficient and productive for the benefit of its customers.  In the 2019 Rate Case, 
4 
the revenue requirements reflected more than $36 million of efficiency savings 
5 
in FY 2023 (nine months of which encompassed the Historic Test Year) through 
6 
traditional productivity and targeted savings initiatives.  Recognizing that 
7 
affordability continues to be the paramount concern of customers, National 
8 
Grid once again undertook an aggressive efficiency program, known as the 
9 
Evolution program, challenging itself to look for ways to further reduce costs 
10 
in advance of these rate filings.  This proactive effort has significantly mitigated 
11 
the impact of rising inflation and other economic factors that have increased 
12 
costs across all sectors.  As a result of National Grid’s effort, the revenue 
13 
requirements reflect annual savings to customers of approximately $45 million 
14 
for KEDNY. 
15 
 
16 
The level of savings from the Evolution program far exceeds the productivity 
17 
savings typically included in a one-year case but continues National Grid’s 
18 
trend of striving to keep customer bills as low as possible.  In the recently 
19 
concluded Management Audit in Case 18-M-0195, Staff commended National 
20 
Grid for undertaking such comprehensive cost-savings initiatives.  While 
21 


--- Page 83 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 80 of 132 
inflation and the need to invest in new programs to meet the CLCPA will 
1 
undoubtedly challenge National Grid’s ability to achieve these savings, 
2 
KEDNY is nevertheless reflecting the full forecast of aspirational savings to 
3 
mitigate rate impacts during this challenging time.  On top of these savings, 
4 
KEDNY is also including a one percent productivity adjustment totaling 
5 
approximately $32 million over the four-year term of the proposed rate plan to 
6 
further mitigate customer bills.     
7 
    
8 
Q. 
Please describe the Evolution Program. 
9 
A. 
In FY 2022, National Grid undertook an ambitious efficiency challenge called 
10 
the Evolution program, which set an aspirational, three-year cumulative 
11 
efficiency goal of $196 million across the New York business by FY 2024.  The 
12 
target is measured against a baseline of FY 2020 performance.  The Evolution 
13 
program was aimed at improving both the quality and cost-effectiveness of 
14 
National Grid’s services to customers.  This ambitious target was purposefully 
15 
set to challenge the business and drive maximum customer value.     
16 
 
17 
Q. 
Why did National Grid undertake this initiative? 
18 
 A. 
Affordability is a significant concern for customers and is a key tenant of 
19 
National Grid’s vision and purpose.  At the same time, the Company needs to 
20 
make investments in new programs and technologies to meet the changing 
21 


--- Page 84 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 81 of 132 
energy landscape and the heightened expectations of customers, regulators, 
1 
policy makers, and other stakeholders.  These include investments to replace 
2 
outdated systems, enhance the safety of the gas network, implement new digital 
3 
solutions, increase energy efficiency and demand response, and enable 
4 
renewable energy sources to meet the goals of the CLCPA.  The need for these 
5 
investments must be balanced against the financial impacts on customers. The 
6 
Evolution program is National Grid’s effort to address these potentially 
7 
competing priorities.  Through the program National Grid has identified 
8 
efficiencies to enable ongoing critical investments and support the State’s long-
9 
term policy and sustainability objectives, while mitigating customers’ energy 
10 
costs in a manner that maintains affordability.   
11 
 
12 
Q. 
How is National Grid attempting to achieve its efficiency target? 
13 
A. 
National Grid undertook a variety of initiatives across its New York electric 
14 
and gas businesses to reduce costs or standardize processes for more efficient 
15 
operations.  Example initiatives include programs that: 
16 
 
17 
 Implement digital strategies to increase customer self-service and 
18 
enhance the overall customer experience;  
19 
 Improve first call resolution in the call centers; 
20 
 Optimize office space; 
21 


--- Page 85 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 82 of 132 
 Update contract strategies to reduce contractor costs; and 
1 
 Utilize new technologies to drive field force efficiencies. 
2 
 
3 
The Evolution program initiatives are being tracked in a web-based tool, known 
4 
as Enterprise Hub (“EHub”).  EHub delineates various maturity stages through 
5 
which initiatives progress as well as confidence levels for delivering forecast 
6 
benefits.  A centralized repository for identifying and tracking the progress of 
7 
the Evolution program initiatives provides transparency to National Grid 
8 
leadership on the progress against targets and avoids overlap in counting 
9 
benefits. 
10 
 
11 
Q. 
Please explain the maturity stages used to track progress in EHub. 
12 
A. 
Each Evolution program initiative is placed at a maturity stage based on its level 
13 
of development.  There are four maturity stages: 
14 
 Identify – This is the initial stage.  Here, initiatives are little more than 
15 
ideas with high-level, conceptual estimates of potential benefits. 
16 
 Define – Teams refine the initiative from an idea to a more formalized 
17 
concept.  Plans are put in place to implement the initiative and refine 
18 
potential benefits.   
19 
 Deliver – The business has begun implementing the initiative.  Savings 
20 
amounts, which could have changed from the original estimate, are 
21 


--- Page 86 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 83 of 132 
quantified and tracked and reviewed by Finance.  There is a line of sight 
1 
to the delivery of future benefits and improvements.     
2 
 Realize – In the final stage, implementation is completed, and the 
3 
improvements and benefits are being sustained.  Actual realized savings 
4 
have been confirmed by Finance.   
5 
Q. 
What was the process used to develop Evolution program initiatives? 
6 
A. 
National Grid’s leadership challenged the business to be bold and think from 
7 
an improvement mindset.  Teams were encouraged to identify as many potential 
8 
initiatives as possible with the understanding they would be refined as they 
9 
progressed through the maturity stages.  While some initiatives would 
10 
ultimately not yield savings opportunities, many would – and the overall effort 
11 
would benefit customers.   
12 
 
13 
To provide further transparency, teams assigned a confidence level to each 
14 
initiative in EHub.  The confidence level included high, medium, and low 
15 
confidence.  In some cases, the initiative may have a low confidence of 
16 
delivering savings because success could require the business to implement a 
17 
new IT solution or a third-party vendor to agree to new contract terms.  
18 
Confidence levels could change over time, as the teams revised their 
19 
assessments 
and 
initiatives 
progressed. 
 
For 
example, 
following 
20 


--- Page 87 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 84 of 132 
implementation, anticipated user adoption could be lower than expected or 
1 
unforeseen challenges may have arisen that changed the initial benefit 
2 
assumptions.  Specific to the Procurement function, because of the complexity 
3 
in tracking procurement benefits, the Procurement team added an additional 
4 
layer of maturity tracking to provide assurance to leadership that actual savings 
5 
had been delivered. 
6 
 
7 
Q. 
Was a governance process established to track Evolution program 
8 
benefits? 
9 
A. 
Yes.  A monthly governance cycle was put in place to track the benefits and 
10 
monitor progress.  Each month, teams update EHub with the latest maturities, 
11 
confidence levels, benefits forecasts, and realized savings.  The results are 
12 
reported monthly to leadership.     
13 
 
14 
Q. 
Please explain how O&M savings from Evolution program initiatives are 
15 
reflected in the case. 
16 
A. 
The Company’s revenue requirement reflects O&M savings associated with 
17 
initiatives it believes are reasonably achievable and likely to deliver customer 
18 
benefits (i.e., those in the “Deliver” and “Realize” maturity stages).  Given the 
19 
immaturity of initiatives in the “Identify” and “Define" maturity stages, the 
20 
Company did not reflect such savings because it is unknown whether the 
21 


--- Page 88 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 85 of 132 
initiatives will be implemented, and, if they are, the extent to which any savings 
1 
will materialize.  Similarly, within Procurement’s Supply Chain Optimization 
2 
initiatives, only underlying procurement opportunities with high maturity levels 
3 
(“Benefits Approved” and “Carry Over”) were reflected.  In addition, the 
4 
Company took a broad approach to including savings in the revenue 
5 
requirements.  In instances where the Rate Year forecast for an initiative was 
6 
lower than the savings reflected in the Historic Test Year, the Company did not 
7 
make a normalizing adjustment to lower the amount of savings.  Instead, the 
8 
Company retained the higher Historic Test Year amounts.

Q. 
Please explain how tax rates are established. 
19 
A. 
Tax rates are set by local taxing jurisdictions (school district, city, county, town, 
20 
special district) for each tax year.  Each jurisdiction determines its revenue from 
21 


--- Page 101 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 98 of 132 
all sources other than property taxes, such as state aid, sales tax revenue, and 
1 
user fees.  Those revenues are subtracted from the jurisdiction’s budget and the 
2 
remainder becomes the property tax levy.  In most cases, to determine the actual 
3 
tax rate, the taxing jurisdiction divides the tax levy by the total taxable assessed 
4 
value of all property in the jurisdiction. 
5 
 
6 
Q. 
How did the Company calculate the average tax rate for the Historic Test 
7 
Year? 
8 
A.   
The Company calculated its average tax rate for the Historic Test Year in three 
9 
steps. 
10 
1. The Company identified all tax parcels for which the Company paid 
11 
property taxes, including the location of the parcel, its assessed value, 
12 
the equalization rate of the municipality where each parcel is located, 
13 
and the taxes paid.  
14 
2. The Company then divided the assessed value of each parcel by the 
15 
applicable equalization rate for the municipality, as established by 
16 
ORPTS, to calculate 100 percent of taxable value for each property. 
17 
3. Finally, the Company divided the total property taxes paid by the 
18 
result of step two above. 
19 
 
20

Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY)

5

17

18 
informal negotiations, it can and does pursue litigation.

Over the years, the Company has successfully contested a number of matters, 
1

3 
special franchise property.

Q. 
What is obsolescence and how does it affect property taxes? 
6 
A. 
Obsolescence is an impairment in the value of an asset that is distinct from 
7 
physical depreciation.  The RCNLD methodology used by ORPTS to develop 
8 
assessments recognizes the existence of functional and economic obsolescence.  
9 
To date, the economic obsolescence allowed by ORPTS is based on the 
10 
Company not achieving certain economic performance metrics.  If these metrics 
11 
improve, the amount of economic obsolescence allowed by ORPTS will 
12 
decrease, causing a corresponding increase in assessments and property taxes. 
13

Q. 
Is the Company proposing a modification to the current reconciliation 
11

12 
A. 
Yes.  The current rate plans provide for variances from the rate allowance for 
13

14

15

17 
KEDNY. 
18 
 
19 
  
The Company is proposing to modify this mechanism.  Given the variability, 
20 
uncertainty, and difficulties associated with forecasting property tax expense, 
21 


--- Page 106 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 103 of 132 
the Company believes that modifying the current reconciliation mechanism to 
1 
a fully symmetrical reconciliation mechanism is both reasonable and 
2 
appropriate.  Municipalities’ economic instability impacting assessments and 
3 
tax levies, difficulty in forecasting the impact of a new rate plan on 
4 
obsolescence, and other factors outside the Company’s control (e.g., New York 
5 
City shifting tax levies among classes), all make forecasting property tax 
6 
expense particularly difficult.  Because KEDNY could continue to experience 
7 
property tax expenses significantly above or below forecast levels, the 
8 
Company believes that customers and the Company would be better protected 
9 
by a full reconciliation mechanism. 
10 
 
11 
Q. 
How does the Company propose to structure the reconciliation 
12 
mechanism? 
13 
A. 
The Company proposes to recover or refund the difference between actual 
14 
property tax expense and the rate allowance through the proposed Rate 
15 
Adjustment Mechanism, which is discussed in the Rate Design Panel’s 
16 
testimony. 
17 
 
18 
Q. 
Why is surcharge recovery appropriate? 
19 
A. 
The difficulties inherent in forecasting property tax expense have contributed 
20 
to more than $38 million of property tax under-collection in recent years.  
21 


--- Page 107 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 104 of 132 
Under-collected property tax expense is the third largest regulatory asset for 
1 
KEDNY at approximately $30 million.  Including property tax expense in the 
2 
Rate Adjustment Mechanism would enable more current recovery of this large 
3 
expense, helping to reduce financing pressure and ensure adequate credit 
4 
metrics.  At the same time, customers will benefit through a sur-credit if the 
5 
reconciliation results in an overcollection.    
6 
 
7 
Q. 
You mentioned that there is a difficulty in forecasting property taxes.  
8 
Please elaborate on that difficulty. 
9 
A. 
As we mentioned previously, property tax valuation is based on the RCNLD 
10 
method.  With the recently experienced increases in inflation, supply chain 
11 
disruptions, and price increases in materials such as pipes and equipment, it has 
12 
become increasingly difficult to forecast the valuation of property.  If inflation 
13 
increases over time, the valuations will become higher.  On the other hand, if 
14 
inflation were to abate, valuations in the future will be more moderate.  Under 
15 
these circumstances, a fully symmetrical property tax reconciliation mechanism 
16 
with recovery or refund through the Rate Adjustment Mechanism is the fairest 
17 
result for both the Company and its customers. 
18 
 
19 


--- Page 108 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 105 of 132 
Q. 
Would a fully symmetrical reconciliation discourage the Companies from 
1 
mitigating property tax expense?  
2 
A. 
No.  As discussed earlier in the Panel’s testimony, the Company has a long 
3 
history of aggressively seeking to minimize property tax assessments.  This 
4 
includes efforts to work with ORPTS to aggressively pursue adjustments to 
5 
obsolescence, litigation with taxing authorities, and challenging unfair 
6 
assessments and unlawful tax charges.  Even with a reconciliation mechanism, 
7 
the Company is incented to continue aggressively pursuing tax mitigation 
8 
measures in the interest of maintaining affordability and cost competitiveness, 
9 
as well as potentially sharing in any tax savings achieved through litigation.  
10 
Moreover, given the variability and uncertainty discussed above, a full and 
11 
symmetrical property tax reconciliation mechanism also serves to protect the 
12 
interests of customers from forecast variations.

Q.

5

6

17

18

Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY)

Q. 
Please explain the “Federal Tax Rate Change 2018” (excess ADIT) item 
1 
the Company included in FIT expense.   
2 
A. 
In 2017, as a result of the enactment of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (the “Act”) 
3 
the federal income tax rate was reduced from 35 percent to 21 percent, which 
4 
was effective for the Company in April 2017.  The deferred tax impact of this 
5 
change (excess ADIT) is being amortized in rates in accordance with the 
6 
method prescribed in the tax regulations and ordered by the Commission. The 
7 
Rate Year and Data Years include the amortization of excess federal ADIT for 
8 
the benefit of customers.  This amortization reduces the Company’s effective 
9 
tax rate and mitigates the rate increase to customers. 
10 
 
11 
Q. 
Please explain how the annual federal excess ADIT amortization was 
12 
calculated. 
13 
A. 
The Company has split the excess ADIT between protected plant, unprotected 
14 
plant, net operating loss (“NOL”), and unprotected non-plant balances.  The 
15 
split between protected plant and unprotected plant was determined following 
16 
the application of a deferred tax module to the tax depreciation system, 
17 
PowerTax.  Protected plant excess ADIT relates to the temporary differences 
18 
between book and tax depreciation methods and lives only.  The Internal 
19 
Revenue Service’s normalization regulations require the Average Rate 
20 
Assumption Method (“ARAM”) to be used to calculate the return of protected 
21 


--- Page 111 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 108 of 132 
excess ADIT if the Company has the data available to implement ARAM.  The 
1 
PowerTax system is able to quantify the ARAM amortization for protected 
2 
plant excess ADIT by applying the current book depreciation rates against the 
3 
tax basis.  The Company has a forecast of ARAM amortization for the Rate 
4 
Year and Data Years from PowerTax.  This amount is reflected in Exhibit __ 
5 
(RRP-6), Summary, Workpaper 4. 
6 
 
7 
 
Unprotected plant excess ADIT is a result of book and tax basis differences 
8 
such as the repair deduction and contributions in aid of construction and other 
9 
plant-related temporary differences such as the current tax deduction for cost of 
10 
removal spending.  The Company proposes to continue to use an amortization 
11 
period of five years to return the unprotected balances to customers. As of the 
12 
end of the Rate Year the entire balance of the unprotected Excess ADIT is 
13 
expected to be returned to customers. The NOL unfunded ADIT is classified as 
14 
a protected asset, as it was the difference between book and tax depreciation, 
15 
including bonus depreciation, that caused the Company to be in an NOL 
16 
position.  The Company proposes to continue to amortize the unfunded NOL 
17 
ADIT in the same amount as the protected plant amortization until it is fully 
18 
utilized.

amortization amounts.

Q. 
What is the Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax? 
1 
A. 
By the enactment of § 10101 of Public Law 117-169, 136 Stat. 1818, 1818-
2 
1828 (August 16, 2022), commonly referred to as the Inflation Reduction Act 
3 
of 2022 (IRA), a new corporate alternative minimum tax (CAMT) was added 
4 
to the Internal Revenue Code (IRC). The CAMT imposes a 15 percent tax on 
5 
the Adjusted Financial Statement Income (AFSI) of applicable corporations for 
6 
taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022. The CAMT is the excess of 
7 
a tentative minimum tax (15 percent of AFSI) over regular tax for the taxable 
8 
year. The applicable corporation is defined as a corporation whose average 
9 
annual AFSI for the three-taxable-year-period ending with the taxable year 
10 
exceeds $1,000,000,000 (general AFSI test) or, in the case of a corporation that 
11 
is a member of a foreign-parented multinational group, is at least $100,000,000 
12 
(foreign-parented multinational group AFSI test).  The CAMT can be claimed 
13 
as a credit against the excess of regular tax over CAMT in future years. 
14 
 
15 
Q. 
Is the Company expected to be subject to CAMT? 
16 
A. 
The Company is a member of a foreign-parented multinational group and has 
17 
AFSI in excess of $100,000,0000; therefore, the Company expects to be subject 
18 
to the CAMT. A “foreign-parented multinational group” is defined as two or 
19 
more entities included in the same applicable financial statement with at least 
20 
one entity being a domestic corporation and another entity being a foreign 
21 


--- Page 121 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 118 of 132 
corporation and the common parent of such entities is a foreign corporation. 
1 
The Company is a domestic corporation included in the same financial 
2 
statement as another foreign corporation and its common parent is a foreign 
3 
corporation. 
4 
 
5 
Q. 
How was CAMT and credit carryforward calculated? 
6 
A. 
The Company first derived AFSI by making the following adjustments to the 
7 
pre-tax book income: 1) deduction for state and local income taxes, 2) reversal 
8 
of book depreciation expense and 3) deduction for accelerated tax depreciation 
9 
under the Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (“MACRS”).  The 
10 
Company applied a 15 percent tax rate to the resulting AFSI to derive tentative 
11 
minimum tax.  The Company then compared the tentative minimum tax to the 
12 
regular tax and derived excess.  The excess of tentative minimum tax over 
13 
regular tax in each Rate Year and Data Years is an increase to income tax 
14 
liability. This excess also constitutes the CAMT credit carryforward available 
15 
to offset regular tax in future years. 
16 
 
17 
Q.  
Why and how was CAMT Credit carryforward included in ADIT? 
18 
A. 
The Company included a deferred tax asset for the estimated CAMT credit 
19 
carryforward as part of other discrete adjustments to rate base ADIT. Because 
20 
CAMT increases income tax liability in the Rate Year and Data Years but is 
21 


--- Page 122 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 119 of 132 
available for carryforward as an offset to regular tax in the future years, it results 
1 
in a deferred tax asset. The deferred tax asset is expected to be realized in future 
2 
years when the regular tax will exceed the minimum tax and the credit 
3 
carryforward can be utilized.  The Company does not expect the estimated 
4 
CAMT credit carryforward to be utilized against regular tax in the Rate Year or 
5 
Data Years.  Therefore, the balance of the deferred tax asset is included in ADIT 
6 
balance and rate base in the Rate Year and Data Years. 
7

Q. 
How did the Company reflect changes in regulatory assets and liabilities in 
9 
the forecast? 
10 
A. 
Because the change in most regulatory assets and liabilities results in a book-
11 
tax timing difference, the existing deferred tax balances on the regulatory 
12 
accounts included in rate base were adjusted by any forecasted change in those 
13 
accounts in the Rate Year and Data Years. 
14 
 
15 
Q. 
Please explain the proration adjustment as it relates to the forecast of 
16 
movement in accumulated deferred federal and state income tax.  
17 
A. 
Section 1.167(1)-1(h)(6) of the federal income tax regulations provides 
18 
requirements for the amount of reserve for deferred income tax that is included 
19 
as a reduction to rate base in a rate filing.  Part (ii) of this subsection requires a 
20 
proration of monthly deferred tax amounts if the rates relate to a “future” period.  
21 


--- Page 123 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel (KEDNY) 
Page 120 of 132 
Proration is not, however, required for a “historic” period.  “Future” periods are 
1 
forecast periods after the date rates go into effect.  “Historic” periods are all 
2 
periods before the effective date for rates even if the underlying data is an 
3 
estimate.  In the filing, deferred tax balances are projected for each Rate Year.   
4 
 
5 
 
The date the new rates go into effect for each rate year begins a “future” period, 
6 
so the movement in the accumulated deferred income tax from that date onward 
7 
is subject to proration. 
8 
 
9 
The pro rata portion is determined by multiplying the monthly changes in 
10 
deferred tax by a fraction, the numerator of which is the number of days 
11 
remaining in the future period at each month’s end and the denominator of 
12 
which is the total number of days in the future period.  Only the movement in 
13 
ADIT changes for the difference between book and tax depreciation net of NOL 
14 
is subject to proration. 
15

b. 2013 – 2016 Deferrals 
 
 
In 2013, the City/State Construction deferral mechanism was eliminated and KEDNY’s 
capital tracker mechanism was modified to a downward-only net utility plant reconciliation 
mechanism that includes allocated common plant and depreciation expense.2  To the extent that 
KEDNY’s net utility plant, inclusive of allocated common plant and depreciation expense, falls 
below the combined target average net utility plant and depreciation expense revenue 
requirement, KEDNY is required to establish a regulatory liability for the benefit of customers.  
KEDNY is not permitted to establish a regulatory asset for any increase in the revenue 
requirement that results from the actual net utility plant and depreciation expense exceeding the 
targets.  The mechanism was originally established to operate on a cumulative basis over the 
two-year term ending December 31, 2014 but was extended to four years by the Commission.3  
In October 2015, the Commission modified KEDNY’s capital investment plan for 2015 and 
2016, allowing KEDNY to use its deferred credit balance as of December 31, 2014 to offset the 
revenue requirement associated with its increased capital expenditures in 2015 and 2016.4

c. 2017 – 2020 Deferrals 
The Joint Proposal in Case 16-G-0059 established two capital trackers for KEDNY: (i) 
the City/State Construction Tracker and (ii) the Net Utility Plant and Depreciation Expense 
Reconciliation Mechanism. 
 City/State Construction Tracker – Section 6.2.2 of the Joint Proposal in Case 16-G-
0059 requires that, to the extent that KEDNY’s actual capital spending for City/State 
construction, net of reimbursements, differs from the forecast amount in a Rate Year, 
KEDNY defers the revenue requirement effect (excluding O&M expenses) associated 
with 90 percent of the difference.   
 Net Utility Plant and Depreciation Reconciliation – Pursuant to Section 6.2.1 of the 
Joint Proposal in Case 16-G-0059, KEDNY implemented a downward only Net 
Utility Plant and Depreciation Expense Reconciliation Mechanism.  Each Rate Year, 
KEDNY reconciles its actual average net utility plant and depreciation expense 
revenue requirement to the target average net utility plant and depreciation expense 
revenue requirement.  The deferred balance is carried forward each Rate Year and 
summed at the end of the third Rate Year.  If at the end of the third Rate Year the 
cumulative balance results in a regulatory liability, the Company defers the revenue 
requirement impact for the benefit of the customers.  If the cumulative balance results 
in a regulatory asset, no deferral is recorded.  In years that incremental Leak Prone 
Pipe replacement costs are recovered through the Gas Safety and Reliability 
Surcharge, the net plant and depreciation components of the Gas Safety and 
Reliability Surcharge for incremental LPP replacement costs are added to the overall 
Net Utility Plant and Depreciation Expense Mechanism target to avoid any double

recovery.  Similarly, in years the City/State Construction Tracker mechanism applies, 
the net plant and depreciation components of the City/State Construction Tracker will 
adjust the overall Net Utility Plant and Depreciation Expense Mechanism target to 
avoid any double recovery.  As of January 1, 2020, the Net Utility Plant and 
Depreciation Expense Reconciliation Mechanism will be converted into a two-way 
tracker until the earlier of the approval of new KEDNY rates via a general rate case or 
June 30, 2020.

 In accordance Section 6.1.1 of the Joint Proposal in Case 16-G-0059, the  
 
Commission authorized KEDNY to continue to defer and reconcile its actual pension  
 
and OPEB expenses to the levels allowed in rates.  
 
Carrying charges are not calculated on pension or OPEB deferred balances. For  
 
purposes of determining KEDNY’s internal reserve and the carrying costs that apply  
 
to that reserve, KEDNY is authorized to combine the funding of its pensions and  
 
OPEBs.  KEDNY accrues and defers carrying charges on the net unfunded pension  
 
and OPEBs amounts, until the net unfunded amount is funded. 
Actual Deferral through December 31, 2022 
 
The deferred balance as of December 31, 2022 was a credit of $15.323 million. 
 
Forecast of Deferral through March 31, 2024 
As of March 31, 2024, the forecast deferral balance is a credit of $15.323 million. 
 
33.  
Rate Plan Deferral Credit 
Basis for the Deferral 
Pursuant to Section 2.2 of the Joint Proposal in Case 19-G-0309, in order to achieve no 
revenue increase in Rate Year 1 and annual increases of 2.0 percent in Rate Years 2 and 
3, KEDNY deferred and amortized $94.873 million of net regulatory liabilities over the 
term of the rate plan. 
Actual Deferral through December 31, 2022 
 
The deferred balance as of December 31, 2022 was a credit of $13.418 million. 
 
Forecast of Deferral through March 31, 2024 
As of March 31, 2024, the forecast deferral balance is a credit of  $4.800 million.

34.  
Reconnect Fees 
Basis for the Deferral 
Pursuant to Section 8.2.8 of the Joint Proposal in Case 19-G-0309, KEDNY will be 
permitted to defer for future recovery from customers any reconnect fees waived for 
customers participating in the Energy Affordability Programs.  
Actual Deferral through December 31, 2022 
 
The deferred balance as of December 31, 2022 was a credit of $0.332 million. 
 
Forecast of Deferral through March 31, 2024 
As of March 31, 2024, the forecast deferral balance is a credit of $0.332 million. 
 
35.  
Service Line Deferral 
Basis for the Deferral 
Inside Service Line Penalty revenue, as described in Section 5.8 of the Joint Proposal in 
Case 19-G-0309,  which KEDNY defers to the benefit of customers.  
Actual Deferral through December 31, 2022 
 
The deferred balance as of December 31, 2022 was a credit of $4.719 million. 
 
Forecast of Deferral through March 31, 2024 
As of March 31, 2024, the forecast deferral balance is a credit of $4.721 million.

Executive summary 
In preparation for Brooklyn Union Gas Company d/b/a National Grid NY (“KEDNY”) and KeySpan Gas East 
Corporation d/b/a National Grid (“KEDLI”) (collectively, the “Companies”) rate case filing, a detailed and 
thorough review of the test year transactions (“Financial Review”) was performed.  
This document outlines the testing approach and results of the Financial Review of test year transactions incurred 
by the Companies, led by internal resources within the National Grid Finance Team (the “Finance Team”).  
Scope of our examination 
Our examination is designed to cover subject matter that includes transactions recorded by the following 
subsidiaries of the National Grid USA (“NGUSA”):  
 
KEDNY 
 
KEDLI 
 
Service Company 
For each entity, the Financial Review report comprises of a Summary of Selected Vendor Costs, a Summary of 
Selected Labor Costs, Employee Expense Costs, and Manual Journal Entries for the twelve-month period ended 
December 31, 2022. 
Risk and approach  
The Finance Team performed a sampling and testing approach consistent with the manner performed for prior 
cases filed with the New York State Public Service Commission to address the risks identified in each area of 
testing.   
Our testing approach was designed to mirror that of an independent external audit. Though the Financial Review 
is being performed by National Grid employees, and is therefore not fully independent, the test is not being 
performed by those who have operated the related controls, nor by those who recorded the related transactions 
and therefore does have a substantial degree of independence from business process owners.   
Results and findings  
Our results and findings are detailed in the Results and Findings section. The findings include net amounts of 
$(0.225) million related to KEDNY (See section “Results and Findings - KEDNY”), $0.009 million related to 
KEDLI (See section “Results and Findings - KEDLI”), and $(1.09) million related to Service Company (See 
section “Results and Findings - Service Company”).

Risk and approach 
The subject matter included in the Summary of Costs reports was developed as follows: 
Vendor costs – The population for testing for vendor costs was from a list of amounts approved for payment 
to each vendor in each of the four quarters of calendar year 2022.  Items were selected for testing using a 
risk-based sampling approach to achieve coverage over unique transactions and vendors. A unique 
transaction was defined as a vendor’s work for a particular project with a particular department at National 
Grid (e.g., If a vendor was performing work for one department under ten different projects, they would 
each be considered a unique transaction of which the Finance Team would obtain 40 percent coverage [i.e. 
4 projects]).  A minimum of 10 percent of the number of invoices associated with each of the unique 
transactions selected for testing would also be examined.  Vendors with transactions that aggregated to less 
than $100,000 thousand dollars were considered de minimis and therefore, not sampled. 
Labor costs (KEDNY & KEDLI) – The population for testing for labor costs was based on a financial 
report which included base time and overtime pay but excluded labor-related overhead costs such as social 
security taxes, life insurance, pensions, post-retirement benefits other than pension, medical, dental and 
other welfare expenses. All relevant base time and overtime pay was selected for inclusion in the population 
and subject to analytical procedures.     
Labor costs (Service Company) – The population for testing for labor costs was based on a financial 
report which included base time and overtime pay but excluded labor-related overhead costs such as social 
security taxes, life insurance, pensions, post-retirement benefits other than pension, medical, dental and 
other welfare expenses. Given the large volume of transactions, items were selected that represented (i) the 
15 largest cost centers based on payroll costs incurred and (ii) 25 cost centers selected without bias ranked 
greater than 15. 
Employee expense costs – The population for testing for employee expense costs was based on a financial 
report of amounts approved for payment in each quarter. Items were selected that represent the top 25 single 
employee claims (“trip reports”) and top 50 purchase credit card (“P-card”) transactions based on dollars 
approved for payment in each quarter, 15 trip reports selected without bias ranked between 26 and 100 
based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter, 10 trip reports selected without bias ranked greater 
than 100 based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter, and 25 P-card transactions selected without 
bias ranked greater than 50 based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter. The Summary of 
Selected Employee Expense Costs did not include any expenses submitted for reimbursement by “Band A” 
employees, defined as senior executives of NGUSA, as well as other costs which were excluded following 
a keyword search – as these costs are not sought for recovery by the Companies.  
General ledger entries – Testing for manual journal entries was based on a financial report of all journal 
entries that impacted manual journal accounts. For each system “document type” included in the list, items 
were identified for selection and presentation in the Summary of Selected General Ledger Entries based on 
dollar value, as detailed in the Notes to each of the Summary of Costs reports.

Cost area
Test objective 
Test details 
Vendor
costs
To test the financial records that 
vendor costs are incurred and 
accurate
1. Compare costs recorded in the ledger to underlying 
vendor support (invoice or similar). 
To test the financial records that 
vendor costs are allocated to the 
correct company 
2. Review the underlying vendor information for details 
of goods purchased or services performed and 
identify whether the goods or services relate to / 
benefit the entity to which they were charged.
To test the financial records that 
costs related to capital programs or 
operating 
expenses 
are 
appropriately classified
3. Review the underlying vendor information for details 
of whether goods purchased, or services performed 
related to a capital program or not. 
Labor
costs
To ensure that payroll costs 
charged through Service Company 
orders and allocated to KEDNY & 
KEDLI are consistent with work 
performed
4. Review amounts charged by employees charging 
Service Company “X” orders and test whether the 
allocation charged is consistent with the employee’s 
job title and functional area. 
To ensure that labor costs charged 
directly to KEDNY & KEDLI are 
accurate 
5. For the 12-month period, review time capture records 
of outlier entries (e.g. more than 12 hours in a day, 
hours worked between midnight and 4 am, multiple 
entries  charged in a day, order/region/segment/ 
company charged  which is inconsistent with the 
employee’s job title and  functional area). Inquiry 
procedures were performed to investigate outliers.
Employee
expenses
To test the financial records that 
employee expenses are accurate 
and submitted consistent with the 
Company policy 
6. Perform a keyword search over the entire employee 
expense population to identify expenses which are 
not being sought for recovery. 
7. Obtain the expense report information and supporting 
documents submitted; compare such documents to 
the requirements of the Company policy, including  
verification that the expenses are allocated to the  
correct general ledger account and order based on the  
employee’s job title and functional area. 
Journal
entries
To test the financial records that 
the journal entries presented are 
accurately calculated and reflect 
the underlying transaction 
8. Obtain copies of the approved journal entry 
submission and test that the entry ties to the 
underlying support. Review elements of the 
underlying support to validate its accuracy and that 
costs are appropriately classified.

Note: NGUSA’s procedures were designed, among other things, to ensure that costs included in the subject 
matter existed during the period. With respect to accrual cut-off, a test of existence is a test for improperly under-
accrued costs at the beginning of the period and improperly over-accrued costs at the end of the period, our 
procedures were not designed to test the completeness of costs contemplated for the subject matter.

Notes to the Summary of Costs 
1.Background 
 
a. KEDNY 
 
 
The Brooklyn Union Gas Company d/b/a National Grid NY (“KEDNY”) distributes natural gas to retail 
customers in the boroughs of Brooklyn, Staten Island, and two-thirds of the borough of Queens, all in New 
York City.  
 
KEDNY is a wholly-owned subsidiary of KeySpan Corporation, which is a wholly-owned subsidiary of 
National Grid USA (“NGUSA”).  NGUSA is a public utility holding company with regulated subsidiaries 
engaged in the generation of electricity and the transmission, distribution, and sale of both natural gas and 
electricity.  NGUSA is a direct wholly-owned subsidiary of National Grid North America Inc. (“NGNA”) and 
an indirect wholly-owned subsidiary of National Grid plc, a public limited company incorporated under the 
laws of England and Wales. 
 
KEDNY separately issues financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting requirements of the 
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) as set forth in its applicable Uniform System of Accounts 
and published accounting releases (together, the “FERC USoA”), as well as financial statements prepared in 
accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States (“GAAP”).  The subject matter 
presented in the Summary of Costs is prepared consistent with the “Basis of Accounting” described in notes 2 
to 5 below, which are not necessarily the same as the accounting requirements of the FERC USoA or GAAP. 
 
b. KEDLI 
 
 
KeySpan Gas East Corporation d/b/a National Grid  (“KEDLI”) distributes natural gas to customers in Nassau 
and Suffolk counties in Long Island, New York, and the Rockaway Peninsula in Queens, New York.  
 
KEDLI is a wholly-owned subsidiary of KeySpan Corporation, which is a wholly-owned subsidiary of 
NGUSA. NGUSA is a public utility holding company with regulated subsidiaries engaged in the generation of 
electricity and the transmission, distribution, and sale of both natural gas and electricity.  NGUSA is a direct 
wholly-owned subsidiary of NGNA and an indirect wholly-owned subsidiary of National Grid plc, a public 
limited company incorporated under the laws of England and Wales. 
 
KEDLI separately issues financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting requirements of 
FERC as set forth in its FERC USoA, as well as financial statements prepared in accordance with GAAP.  The 
subject matter presented in the Summary of Costs is prepared consistent with the “Basis of Accounting” 
described in notes 2 to 5 below, which are not necessarily the same as the accounting requirements of the FERC 
USoA or GAAP. 
 
c. Service Company 
 
National Grid USA Service Company (“Service Company”) provides management, administrative, 
accounting, legal, engineering and other services to NG USA subsidiaries. 
 
Service Company is, a wholly-owned subsidiary of NGUSA, provides management, administrative, 
accounting, legal, engineering, and other services to other NGUSA subsidiaries, including the KEDNY and 
KEDLI. Service Company provides its services on an “at cost” basis, determined using billing methods based 
on cost causative factors pursuant to service agreements and its Cost Allocation Manual, as further discussed 
in Note 6. 
 
 
 
2. Vendor Costs

Summary of Selected Vendor Costs – During each of the quarters in the period from January 1, 2022 to 
December 31, 2022, KEDNY and KEDLI approved payments to third party vendors totaling $786,585,708, 
$322,768,627 and $1,885,055,940 for KEDNY, KEDLI and Service Company (collectively, the 
“Companies”), respectively. The Summary of Selected Vendor Costs represents vendor costs “approved for 
payment” during each of the quarters in the period from January 1, 2022 to December 31, 2022, related to the 
selected vendors listed. Irrespective of when the goods or services were received, for purposes of this 
presentation, vendor costs are considered approved for payment upon: 
 
 
internal acknowledgment that the goods or services have been received, and 
 
payment of the invoice. 
 
The subject matter excludes amounts approved for payment related to purchased commodity as these costs 
generally are not recovered via KEDNY and KEDLI’s base delivery rates. 
 
To capture and account for vendor costs, the Companies initiate work orders under two types of projects, (1) 
capital projects, under which work orders are designed to capture costs incurred in the execution of the 
Company’s capital programs, and (2) expense projects, under which work orders are designed to capture costs 
incurred in the performance of non-capital-related activity. The subject matter and basis of accounting reflects 
the initial determination of whether the vendor costs were assigned to capital projects or expense projects. 
System-generated entries (generally related to the allocation of engineering-related work order design 
adjustments, or the apportionment of overhead) and adjustments to allocate elements of work orders assigned 
to capital projects to expense are not contemplated in the subject matter. 
 
All costs included in the Summary of Selected Vendor Costs have been “approved for payment” by the 
Companies, and properly allocated and charged to the Companies and their affiliates, in accordance with the 
NGUSA’s Cost Allocation Manual. The Cost Allocation Manual is further described in Note 6. Note that 
vendor costs may have been incurred before the period from January 1, 2022 to December 31, 2022, but if 
both elements above were not present until after January 1, 2022 to December 31, 2022, such costs would 
consequently be “approved for payment” during the period presented and included in the accompanying 
Summary of Selected Vendor Costs. Likewise, vendor costs incurred during the period from January 1, 2022 
to December 31, 2022, where both elements above were not present prior to December 31, 2022, are not 
considered “approved for payment” during the period presented, nor included in the accompanying Summary 
of Selected Vendor Costs. This accounting policy, applied in the Summary of Costs, is a basis of accounting 
other than GAAP and the FERC USoA. 
 
Upon satisfaction of the conditions approving a cost for payment, the cost is assigned to a work order as 
follows: 
 
 
Costs incurred in support of the Companies’ capital programs are assigned to work orders capturing 
costs under capital projects. 
 
 
Costs related solely to operating activities are assigned to work orders capturing costs under expense 
projects, or internal orders capturing expense items specific to one of the Companies and incurred 
outside of their respective capital programs.

4. Employee Expense Costs 
 
Summary of Selected Employee Expense Costs – During the period from January 1, 2022 to December 31, 
2022, approved payments to employees as reimbursement for business expenses incurred totaling $2,862,925, 
$1,556,785 and $23,602,005 for KEDNY, KEDLI and Service Company, respectively. Business expenses are 
approved for payment if they are incurred in the normal course of business, in accordance with the Companies’ 
internal policies, and include business travel, accommodation, spot purchases of goods, and other out-of-
pocket expenses. The Summary of Selected Employee Expense Costs includes a subset of such expenses. This 
subject matter, designed to reflect a component of total employee expense costs, was developed as follows. 
The Finance Team obtained a list of amounts approved for payment by the Company in each quarter. Based 
upon this list, items were selected that represent the top 25 single employee claims (“trip reports”) and top 50 
purchase credit card (“P-card”) transactions based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter, 15 trip 
reports selected without bias ranked between 26 and 100 based on dollars approved for payment in each 
quarter, 10 trip reports selected without bias ranked greater than 100 based on dollars approved for payment 
in each quarter, and 25 P-card transactions selected without bias ranked greater than 25 based on dollars 
approved for payment in each quarter. The Summary of Selected Employee Expense Costs also only includes 
expenses submitted by certain employees; it does not include any expenses submitted for reimbursement by 
“Band A” employees, defined as senior executives of NGUSA, as well as other costs which were excluded 
following a keyword search, as these costs are not sought for recovery by the KEDNY or KEDLI. 
 
Irrespective of when the expense was incurred, for purposes of this presentation, employee expenses are 
considered approved for payment upon submission by an employee of a request for reimbursement for a 
business expense, accompanied by evidence of the expense, and recoverable consistent with NGUSA’s US 
Business Travel & Expense Policy, effective January 18, 2011, updated December 8, 2020. This accounting 
policy, applied in the Summary of Costs, is a basis of accounting other than GAAP and the FERC USoA. 
 
All costs included in the accompanying Summary of Selected Employee Expense Costs have been allocated 
to the Company in a manner consistent with the Cost Allocation Manual.
